<reason>Both sides fought a tight, well-framed clash with clean formatting (both used A1:/A2: labels and two real questions). PRO's case rested on two load-bearing mechanisms: (1) ownership/title decides who gets cut in drought, so caps are "a negotiation every dry year," and (2) bottling is uniquely harmful because water leaves the basin as merchandise rather than as an input. CON damaged both. The usufructuary-rights answer [A4.1] — that water rights are conditional permits curtailed routinely under drought clauses, not fee-simple title — directly undercut PRO's central "you must fight a property right" mechanism, and PRO's closing reply ([B5.2] "still a claim that must be argued down") was assertion rather than rebuttal. CON also converted PRO's own concession [B4.4] that volumetric caps bind farms and fabs into a strong consistency attack: caps are trusted against the actors causing most drawdown and distrusted only against the smallest one, which CON memorably called "a theory of villainy" rather than hydrology. CON's closing then dismantled the product-vs-input distinction with virtual water export (almond water also leaves the cycle permanently), a timely response to a distinction PRO first articulated in Rebuttal 2. PRO did real work too: it plausibly closed the "drill eight kilometres away" escape hatch via the aquifer clause, answered the emergency-pallet dilemma reasonably (public treated surface water, desalination, stockpiles, existing inventory), and landed the good point that "a town does not live on basin averages." But PRO's sham-reformulation policing [B4.3] handed CON a clean contradiction against its own capture argument, and PRO never offered a concrete reason why a recharge-tied cap with domestic-first priority fails where its own residual cap regime succeeds. CON made the decisive test — litres out of the ground versus identity of the deed-holder — easier for a reader to apply, so it wins clearly but not overwhelmingly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's usufructuary-rights answer [A4.1]-[A4.2] combined with the exploitation of PRO's concession that caps bind farms and fabs [A4.4]-[A4.5]: it stripped the "property right beats the drought cutoff" mechanism and showed PRO trusting the very tool it called doomed against far larger extractors, a charge PRO never squarely met.</best_rebuttal>
